newsitem.title: SPAIN: Gonzalez asks court to see Spain "dirty war" files.
newsitem.headline: Gonzalez asks court to see Spain "dirty war" files.

text.p: Spain's former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez said on Sunday he wanted to give the courts and legislative bodies access to secret service files, including ones on a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatists.

Gonzalez, whose 13-year Socialist government has been accused of running the campaign of kidnap, torture and murder that killed 28 people from 1983-87, told journalists in Barcelona he would like branches of government other than the executive to see the files.

His administration, like the present conservative regime of Jose Maria Aznar, had refused court requests to declassify the military intelligence files on the "dirty war" death squads, citing reasons of state security.
But Gonzalez said the country had a phobia about state secrets being kept with the executive powers alone.

"One way to overcome this misconception of state security is organising things so that the same documentation that comes to the executive from the secret services can come to the judicial and legislative powers," he said.
Gonzalez said he was tired of fending off accusations that his government had hidden behind the "state security excuse" to cover up past activities.

He has denied any involvement or awareness of the illegal operations against ETA Basque guerrillas but some former security chiefs implicated in the scandal and Aznar's deputy prime minister, Francisco Alvarez Cascos, say he masterminded the secret war.
The Supreme Court is to rule on November 4 whether there is enough evidence to question or charge Gonzalez in connection with the shadowy operation, known as GAL or Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups.

His first interior minister and other high officials are already on trial for involvement with the GAL, which stepped outside the law to stop ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) guerrillas, who were killing about once a week in a fight for Basque independence.
The crucial body of evidence against the former administration is believed to be contained in the secret papers which the government refuses to hand over to the courts.

Left wing opposition leader Julio Anguita says the Socialists have a secret deal with the present Popular Party government to keep the "dirty war" papers out of the courts and he predicts a major upheaval if they were turned over.
Aznar, who used mounting evidence about the GAL to hound the Socialists into holding the elections which brought their defeat in March, has so far thwarted the courts.

Defence Minister Eduardo Serra, an independent, reaffirmed at the weekend that the government's decision not to declassify the files was unshakeable and said he would defy the Supreme Court if it tried to force the issue.
Gonzalez said he wanted to put an end to all speculation by letting the courts review the files.

"All of my relations with the secret services are documented and it seems right that the president(s) of Parliament...the Supreme Court and the Judicial Council should have access to the same information as other state authorities," he said in an interview published in El Pais on Sunday.
